The exact equation rests on every result before it in Appendix A, and Theorem 7 needs only two more: the kernel's lemma and the slope of the flat bound.

This appendix collects every proof in the paper, in the paper's order: the facts and the derivation in Section 2 that the proofs use, the standing facts at the start of Appendix A, its proofs, and Appendix B's bounds for unequal rewards. Each section says what the result proves, what it assumes, and what it uses, then gives the paper's statement and proof in full and the steps a chapter draws for it, with a link to that chapter's live plate. Where the paper takes a fact from other work, or calls an argument formal, the section says so in the paper's terms. Remark 5 and the extensions of Section 7, which the paper argues without proving, are taught in chapters 5 and 11.

Set the dial to Exact or Both to read the paper's text; Plain shows the steps alone. The picture above walks through the same results, with an arc for each use the claim map records.

Facts the proofs use, from Section 2

Section 2 sets up the model every proof works in. The evidence X is half the log odds of the two answers, and its size Y=|X| is a diffusion reflected at 0, with generator L=12∂y2+tanh⁡(y)∂y. The chance that the current choice is right, g(y)=1/(1+e−2y), has no drift while Y>0 (Lg=0), its slope is g′(y)=1/(2cosh2⁡y), and (cosh2⁡yf′)′=2cosh2⁡yLf for any twice differentiable f. The paper states these briefly, and chapter 2 works them out; the equation for X that they start from is cited (Peskir and Shiryaev, 2006, Ch. VI). The excerpt also sets the standing assumption on the cost of time, continuous with 0<cmin≤c(t)≤cmax, and defines the value V(t,y).

In the claim map:

  • It uses Posterior and the filtered diffusion.
  • What uses it: Strong solutions of the reflected equation; The value function; The constant-cost bound B(c); Lemma 1 · Structure; Proposition 3 · Regularity (nondegeneracy, Hölder continuity, smooth fit); Proposition 4 · Exact equation for the bound; The kernel w (survival flux at the bound).
The paper's text, in Section 2

Reward and cost. Deciding at a stopping time τ and choosing sign(Xτ) is correct with conditional probability g(|Xτ|). The cost of time c(t) is continuous, with 0<cmin≤c(t)≤cmax. The decision maker maximizes

(7)E[g(|Xτ|)−∫0τc(s)ds].

By symmetry, it is enough to follow Y=|X|. By Tanaka's formula, Y is the reflected diffusion dY=tanh⁡(Y)dt+dB+dℓ on [0,∞), where B is a Brownian motion and ℓ increases only when Y=0. Its generator is L=12∂y2+tanh⁡(y)∂y with a reflecting boundary at 0. Two facts about g are used throughout: Lg=0 on y>0, because g(X) is a martingale, and g(1−g)=1/(4cosh2⁡y), so g′(y)=1/(2cosh2⁡y). A third is the identity (cosh2⁡yf′)′=2cosh2⁡yLf, valid for any twice differentiable f.

The value of starting at time t with Y=y is

(8)V(t,y)=supτEy[g(Yτ)−∫0τc(t+s)ds].

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 232–250

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 5

Write the belief through tanh, and the product g(1−g) simplifies.

g(y)=1+tanh⁡y2, so g(1−g)=14(1+tanh⁡y)(1−tanh⁡y)=14(1−tanh2⁡y)=14cosh2⁡y.

Step 2 of 5

Differentiate: the slope of the belief is twice that product.

g′=12sech2y=2g(1−g)=12cosh2⁡y, and g″=−sech2ytanh⁡y.

Step 3 of 5

For y>0, the generator's expression sends g to 0: the belief has no drift while Y>0.

Lg=12g″+tanh⁡yg′=−12sech2ytanh⁡y+12tanh⁡ysech2y=0 for y>0. At y=0, the reflection adds g′(0)dℓ=12dℓ, which is where the value of waiting comes from in chapter 4.

Step 4 of 5

Multiplying by cosh2⁡y turns the generator into a single derivative.

(cosh2⁡yf′)′=2cosh⁡ysinh⁡yf′+cosh2⁡yf″=2cosh2⁡y(12f″+tanh⁡yf′)=2cosh2⁡yLf, for any twice differentiable f.

Step 5 of 5

A first use: the mean time for Y to reach a level b.

m(y)=Eyτb solves Lm=−1 on [0,b) with m′(0)=0 (the reflection) and m(b)=0. Step 4 gives (cosh2⁡ym′)′=−2cosh2⁡y, so cosh2⁡ym′=−(y+12sinh⁡2y), which is m′=−(ytanh⁡y)′, and m(y)=btanh⁡b−ytanh⁡y.

Chapter 2 draws each step beside its live plate “Three facts about g”, in Folding the problem in half.

The flat bound and its slope, from Section 2

For a constant cost c, the problem looks the same from every start time, and the best rule stops when Y first reaches a fixed level, B(c). The paper finds the level two ways, from the value's equation with smooth fit and by maximizing the reward of a flat bound, and differentiates the result to get the slope B′(c), which is negative at every cost. These are derivations in the text of Section 2, not proofs in Appendix A, but the appendix uses both, among other places: the flat bound in Lemma 1(c), the optimal-stopping fact, Lemma 6, Corollary 9, Proposition 13, and Proposition 10, and the slope in Theorem 7 and Proposition 13. The claim map, below, records fewer of these uses.

In the claim map, for The constant-cost bound B(c):

  • It uses The reflected process Y = |X|, its generator, and three facts about g; The value function.
  • What uses it: The per-moment rule; The slope of the constant-cost bound; Lemma 1 · Structure; Optimal stopping applies after capping the bound; The kernel w (survival flux at the bound); Lemma 6 · Two descriptions of the kernel; Corollary 9 · Limits (slow changes, mean look-ahead, fast changes); Proposition 10 · Second-order loss.

In the claim map, for The slope of the constant-cost bound:

  • What uses it: Theorem 7 · The first-order theorem.
The derivation, in Section 2

Constant cost. For a constant cost c, the optimal rule stops when Y first reaches a level B(c). In the continuation region, the value solves LV=c with V′(0)=0, so (cosh2⁡yV′)′=2ccosh2⁡y and cosh2⁡yV′(y)=c(y+12sinh⁡2y). Smooth fit at the bound, V′(b)=g′(b)=1/(2cosh2⁡b), then gives

(9)sinh⁡(2b)+2b=1c,

whose root is B(c). The same equation follows from maximizing g(b)−cbtanh⁡b, the expected reward of a flat bound b, since btanh⁡b is the mean decision time. Differentiating (9) gives

(10)B′(c)=−14c2cosh2⁡B(c).

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 252–267

The bound, two ways.

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 5

For a constant cost, the problem looks the same at every start time, so the decision maker stops once Y reaches a flat level b. Below it, the value solves one equation.

LV=c on [0,b), with V′(0)=0 at the reflecting center and V(b)=g(b). For each trial level, the value of following that flat rule, Vb(y)=g(b)−c(btanh⁡b−ytanh⁡y), solves it, since L(ytanh⁡y)=1.

Step 2 of 5

Multiply by 2cosh2⁡y and integrate once from the center: below its own level, every rule has the same slope.

Since (cosh2⁡yf′)′=2cosh2⁡yLf for any smooth f, (cosh2⁡yV′)′=2ccosh2⁡y, so cosh2⁡yVb′(y)=c(y+12sinh⁡2y) on [0,b), for every b.

Step 3 of 5

Smooth fit picks the level: at the bound, the value meets g with the same slope.

V′(b)=g′(b)=12cosh2⁡b makes the left side of step 2 equal 12 at y=b: c(b+12sinh⁡2b)=12, which is sinh⁡(2b)+2b=1/c. Its root is B(c).

Step 4 of 5

The second route: a flat bound b earns g(b) on every decision and pays c for each unit of its mean decision time, btanh⁡b.

From Eyτb=btanh⁡b−ytanh⁡y (chapter 2), the expected reward of a flat bound is R(b)=g(b)−cbtanh⁡b, which is Vb(0).

Step 5 of 5

Set its slope to zero. The same equation comes out, because the reward's slope is the gap between the two slopes at the bound.

R′(b)=g′(b)−c(tanh⁡b+bsech2b)=sech2b[12−c(b+12sinh⁡2b)]. Since c(tanh⁡b+bsech2b)=Vb′(b), R′(b)=g′(b)−Vb′(b): the reward peaks where smooth fit holds.

Chapter 3 draws each step beside its live plate “Two routes, one equation”, in The flat bound, two ways.

Its slope.

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 4

Write the equation as an identity in the cost: B(c) is where the rising curve F(b)=sinh⁡2b+2b meets 1/c.

F(B(c))=1/c for every c>0. F increases from F(0)=0 without limit, so the root is unique.

Step 2 of 4

Differentiate both sides in c, by the chain rule.

F′(B(c))B′(c)=−1c2. (B is differentiable by the implicit function theorem, since F′>0.)

Step 3 of 4

The slope of F is four times a square.

F′(b)=2cosh⁡2b+2, and cosh⁡2b+1=2cosh2⁡b, so F′(b)=4cosh2⁡b.

Step 4 of 4

Divide: the slope of the bound, negative at every cost.

B′(c)=−14c2cosh2⁡B(c)<0: a higher constant cost always means a lower bound.

Chapter 3 draws each step beside its live plate “Differentiating the equation”, in How the bound changes with the cost.

The standing facts, at the start of Appendix A

Appendix A opens with its standing assumptions: the cost is continuous with 0<cmin≤c≤cmax; it is extended to start times in (−1,∞) by c(t)=c(0) for t<0, so that t=0 is an interior time; and only stopping times with a finite mean need be considered, since any other costs infinitely much. Then come two facts the paper calls standard and uses throughout.

Strong solutions is cited: Skorokhod's lemma (Revuz and Yor, 1999, Ch. VI, Lemma 2.1) reflects every continuous path at 0 through a map that is Lipschitz in the supremum norm, and Picard iteration with Gronwall's lemma gives one strong solution from every start. The paper runs every start on the same Brownian motion, so later proofs can compare two starts path by path.

Optimal stopping applies a cited theorem, Peskir and Shiryaev's (2006, Ch. I, Thm. 2.2) for continuous gains, through an argument of the paper's own. The theorem assumes Esups|Gs|<∞, which fails here because the gain is unbounded below, so the paper caps each decision at the flat bound for the lowest cost, b¯=B(cmin), and shows that the cap never lowers the expected gain. The cap uses Lemma 1(b), which the paper proves just after. The conclusion: the first entry into the stopping set, τt,y∗, is optimal, and the value process V(t+s,Ys)−∫0sc(t+u)du, stopped there, is a martingale.

The standing assumptions, in Appendix A

Throughout, the cost is continuous with 0<cmin≤c≤cmax. To make t=0 an interior time, extend the cost to (−1,∞) by c(t)=c(0) for t<0 and define the value for start times in (−1,∞) the same way; this changes nothing at t≥0, and every argument below is applied on the extended interval. It suffices to consider stopping times with Eτ<∞, since the cost of any other is infinite. Two standard facts are used throughout.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 1267–1271

Strong solutions.

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 5

Reflection at 0 is a map on paths: add back the furthest the path has been below 0.

For a continuous path U with U0≥0, Skorokhod's lemma gives the unique pair with Y=U+ℓ≥0 and ℓ nondecreasing from ℓ0=0, growing only when Y=0: ℓt=sups≤t(−Us)+. The map Γ:U↦Y is Lipschitz in the supremum norm, with constant 2.

Step 2 of 5

Picard iteration: reflect, recompute the drift, and reflect again.

Set Yn+1=Γ(y+∫0⋅tanh⁡(Ysn)ds+B). Since tanh is Lipschitz with constant 1, sups≤t|Ysn+1−Ysn|≤2∫0tsupr≤s|Yrn−Yrn−1|ds, so the distances shrink like (2t)n/n! and the iterates converge to a solution.

Step 3 of 5

Gronwall's lemma: the solution is unique, so each start and each noise path give one path.

Two solutions Y,Y~ from the same start on the same B satisfy sups≤t|Ys−Y~s|≤2∫0tsupr≤s|Yr−Y~r|ds, so Y=Y~. The paper runs every start on the same B, so all of them share one filtration.

Step 4 of 5

Two paths that meet are one path from then on, and continuous paths can't pass each other without meeting.

If Ys1=Ys2 at some time s, then after s both solve the same equation from the same point with the same B, and step 3 makes them equal. So for y1≤y2, Yt1≤Yt2 for all t: paths that start ordered stay ordered.

Step 5 of 5

What chapter 4 uses: the lower start collects at least as much local time.

Write Yi=Ui+ℓi. Then U1−U2=y1−y2+∫(tanh⁡Y1−tanh⁡Y2)ds≤0, and since ℓti=sups≤t(−Usi)+, ℓ1≥ℓ2 pathwise.

Chapter 2 draws each step beside its live plate “Two starts, one noise”, in Two starts on the same noise.

Strong solutions, in Appendix A

Strong solutions. Skorokhod's lemma (Revuz and Yor, 1999, Ch. VI, Lemma 2.1) gives a unique reflection at 0 of every continuous path, through a map that is Lipschitz in the supremum norm, and tanh is Lipschitz, so the reflected equation dY=tanh⁡(Y)dt+dB+dℓ has a unique strong solution from every starting point, by Picard iteration and Gronwall's lemma. We run it from every starting point with the same Brownian motion B, so the processes share one filtration.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 1273–1278

Optimal stopping.

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 4

The textbook theorem needs a gain that stays integrable, and this one falls without bound.

The gain from stopping at s is Gs=g(Ys)−∫0sc(t+u)du≤1−cmins, so Esups|Gs|=∞. The theorem for continuous gains (Peskir and Shiryaev, 2006, Ch. I, Thm. 2.2) assumes it is finite.

Step 2 of 4

Cap the decision at the flat bound for the lowest cost; that never lowers the gain.

Let σ be the first time Y≥b¯=B(cmin). From b¯, under any cost of at least cmin, no stopping time earns more than the constant-cost value for cmin (Lemma 1(b)), which is g(b¯). So replacing τ by τ∧σ never lowers the expected gain.

Step 3 of 4

The capped gain is bounded by something with a finite mean.

|Gs∧σ|≤1+cmaxσ, and Eyσ=b¯tanh⁡b¯−ytanh⁡y<∞ for y≤b¯.

Step 4 of 4

Now the theorem applies: the first entry into the stopping set is optimal.

By the Markov property of (t+s,Ys), the Snell envelope of the capped gain is V(t+s,Ys)−∫0sc(t+u)du up to σ. The theorem says its first meeting with the gain, which is τt,y∗ and comes no later than σ, so it is finite, is optimal, and that the Snell envelope, stopped there, is a martingale.

Chapter 4 draws each step beside its live plate “Cap the gain, then use the theorem”, in Why stopping at the bound is optimal.

Optimal stopping, in Appendix A

Optimal stopping. The gain Gs=g(Ys)−∫0sc(t+u)du is continuous but unbounded below, so the theorem for continuous gains (Peskir and Shiryaev, 2006, Ch. I, Thm. 2.2), which assumes Esups|Gs|<∞, does not apply as it stands. It applies after stopping the gain at σ=inf{s≥0:Ys≥b¯}, with b¯=B(cmin); a start at or above b¯ is in the stopping set, so σ=0 there. Stopping there is optimal: from b¯, under any cost of at least cmin, no stopping time earns more than the constant-cost value for cmin (Lemma 1(b)), which equals g(b¯). So replacing τ by τ∧σ never lowers the expected gain, and |Gs∧σ|≤1+cmaxσ with Eyσ=b¯tanh⁡b¯−ytanh⁡y<∞ for y≤b¯. By the Markov property of (t+s,Ys), the Snell envelope of the stopped gain is V(t+s,Ys)−∫0sc(t+u)du up to σ. The theorem then shows that its first meeting with the gain, which is the first entry τt,y∗ into the stopping set and comes no later than σ, is optimal, and that the value process stopped there is a martingale.

Where the text relies on it, in Section 3…

Write

(11)τt,y∗=inf{s≥0:Ys≥b(t+s)},Y0=y,

for the first entry into the stopping set from (t,y); it is an optimal stopping time, by the standing facts at the start of Appendix A.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 305–310

Lemma 1: structure

Four facts that follow from comparison arguments alone: (a) the value of waiting, V−g, falls as the evidence rises, so the stopping set at each time is a ray [b(t),∞); (b) a higher cost gives a lower value and a lower bound; (c) so the bound stays between the flat bounds for the highest and the lowest cost; (d) the value changes with the start time at a rate of at most cmax−cmin, for any bounded measurable cost. The proof is the paper's own. Part (a) compares two starts on one Brownian motion, from the strong-solutions fact, and part (c) uses the flat bound.

In the claim map:

  • It uses The value function; The reflected process Y = |X|, its generator, and three facts about g; Strong solutions of the reflected equation; The constant-cost bound B(c).
  • What uses it: The optimal decision time tau*; Optimal stopping applies after capping the bound; Lemma 2 · Envelope identity; Proposition 3 · Regularity (nondegeneracy, Hölder continuity, smooth fit); Theorem 7 · The first-order theorem; Proposition 10 · Second-order loss.
The statement, in Section 3
Lemma 1 (Structure).
  • (a)

    For each t, y↦V(t,y)−g(y) is nonincreasing, so the stopping set at time t is an interval [b(t),∞).

  • (b)

    If c1≤c2 pointwise, then Vc1≥Vc2 and bc1≥bc2.

  • (c)

    Hence B(cmax)≤b(t)≤B(cmin) for all t.

  • (d)

    |V(t,y)−V(t′,y)|≤(cmax−cmin)|t−t′| for all t,t′,y.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 293–302

Part (a).

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 4

Waiting changes the expected reward only through the push that keeps the evidence off 0.

By Itô's formula, with Lg=0 for y>0 and g′(0)=12: g(Yτ)=g(y)+∫0τg′(Ys)dBs+12ℓτ. The stochastic integral has mean 0 for stopping times with finite mean, so V(t,y)−g(y)=supτEy[12ℓτ−Cτ], where Cτ=∫0τc(t+s)ds is the cost paid.

Step 2 of 4

Two starts on the same noise stay in order, and the lower one collects at least as much local time.

Write Y=U+ℓ, with Us=y+∫0stanh⁡(Yr)dr+Bs and ℓs=supr≤s(−Ur)+. For y1≤y2, paths that meet coincide afterward (pathwise uniqueness), so Y1≤Y2. Then U1≤U2, because y1≤y2 and tanh⁡Y1≤tanh⁡Y2, and Skorokhod's formula gives ℓ1≥ℓ2 path by path.

Step 3 of 4

So every stopping time gains at least as much from the lower start: the value of waiting never rises as the evidence rises.

Under one stopping time τ, the cost Cτ is the same from both starts, so 12ℓτ1−Cτ≥12ℓτ2−Cτ on every path. Take expectations, then suprema: V(t,y1)−g(y1)≥V(t,y2)−g(y2), so y↦V(t,y)−g(y) is nonincreasing.

Step 4 of 4

Where waiting is worth nothing, it is worth nothing higher up: the stopping set is a ray.

V−g≥0, so if it is 0 at y0, it is 0 at every y≥y0: the stopping set at time t is [b(t),∞). It is closed because V is Lipschitz (the same coupling gives 0≤V(t,y2)−V(t,y1)≤12(y2−y1), and part (d) covers time), and it isn't empty, since by part (b) it contains [B(cmin),∞).

Chapter 4 draws each step beside its live plate “Two starts on the same noise”, in One level at each moment.

Parts (b) and (c).

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 4

Use one stopping time for both costs: on every path, the higher cost charges at least as much.

If c1≤c2 at every moment, then, for any stopping time τ, the reward g(Yτ) is the same under both, and ∫0τc1(t+s)ds≤∫0τc2(t+s)ds.

Step 2 of 4

So the higher cost has the lower value.

Every stopping time earns at least as much under c1 as under c2. Taking suprema, Vc1≥Vc2.

Step 3 of 4

A lower value meets the reward for deciding sooner: the stopping set grows, and the bound comes down.

Since V≥g, the stopping set {V=g} grows as V shrinks: where Vc1=g, also Vc2=g. So bc1≥bc2, which is part (b).

Step 4 of 4

Compare with the two constant costs.

cmin≤c(t)≤cmax at every moment, and a constant cost c has the flat bound B(c) at every moment (chapter 3). By part (b), B(cmax)≤b(t)≤B(cmin) for all t, which is part (c).

Chapter 4 draws each step beside its live plate “A higher cost, a lower bound”, in A band the bound can't leave.

Part (d).

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 4

Fix one stopping rule, and start it at two times.

Take t≤t′ (the other case is the same) and a stopping time τ. The evidence path, and so the reward g(Yτ), doesn't depend on the start time; the cost does: ∫0τc(t+s)ds from t, and ∫0τc(t′+s)ds from t′.

Step 2 of 4

The two costs differ only by two stretches of length t′−t.

With C(u)=∫0uc, the cost from t is C(t+τ)−C(t) and from t′ is C(t′+τ)−C(t′). Their difference, regrouped, is ∫t+τt′+τc−∫tt′c, whether or not the two decisions overlap in time.

Step 3 of 4

Each end is an interval of length t′−t.

So each integral lies between cmin(t′−t) and cmax(t′−t), and their difference is at most (cmax−cmin)(t′−t) in size, on every path.

Step 4 of 4

Take the best rule on each side.

A bound that holds for every stopping time holds for the suprema: |V(t,y)−V(t′,y)|≤(cmax−cmin)|t−t′|. Nothing used continuity, so this holds for any bounded measurable cost.

Chapter 4 draws each step beside its live plate “Two start times, one rule”, in How far the value moves with the start time.

The proof, in Appendix A.1

(a) By Itô's formula and Lg=0 on y>0, with g′(0)=12,

(30)g(Yτ)=g(y)+∫0τg′(Ys)dBs+12ℓτ,

so V(t,y)−g(y)=supτEy[12ℓτ−∫0τc(t+s)ds]. By the Skorokhod construction, Y=U+ℓ with Us=y+∫0stanh⁡(Yr)dr+Bs and ℓs=supr≤s(−Ur)+. For y1≤y2, Y1≤Y2: two solutions driven by the same B that meet coincide from then on, by pathwise uniqueness, so paths that start ordered stay ordered. So U1−U2=y1−y2+∫(tanh⁡Y1−tanh⁡Y2)≤0 and therefore ℓ1≥ℓ2 pathwise. Every stopping time earns at least as much from y1 as from y2 in this representation, so V−g at y1 is at least V−g at y2. With a common stopping time, the same coupling gives V(t,y1)≤V(t,y2), since g is increasing, so 0≤V(t,y2)−V(t,y1)≤g(y2)−g(y1)≤12(y2−y1). With (d), V is Lipschitz, so the stopping set is closed.

(b) Use the same stopping time for both costs. Since V≥g, the stopping set {V=g} grows as V shrinks.

(c) Compare with the constant costs cmax and cmin, using (b).

(d) For a fixed stopping time τ, ∫0τc(t′+s)ds−∫0τc(t+s)ds=∫t+τt′+τc−∫tt′c, The two integrals on the right run over intervals of length |t′−t|, so each lies between cmin|t′−t| and cmax|t′−t|, and their difference is at most (cmax−cmin)|t′−t| in absolute value. Take suprema.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 1296–1319

Lemma 2: the envelope identity

Below the bound, the value is smooth in the evidence and continuously differentiable in time, its slope is 0 at the reflecting center, and two identities hold: Vt=c(t)−Ey[c(t+τt,y∗)], and LV=Ey[c(t+τt,y∗)], the expected cost at the moment of decision. The first is an envelope argument: hold the optimal decision time from one start fixed, and move the start time. For the smoothness, the paper solves a Dirichlet problem for a uniformly parabolic operator on rectangles inside the continuation set, citing Peskir and Shiryaev (2006, Sec. 7.1) for the method. Campbell and Engelund (2026) give both identities for smooth terminal losses; their hypotheses exclude this model's 0-1 loss, so the paper proves them directly (Section 8).

The statement, in Section 3
Lemma 2 (Envelope identity).

At every point (t,y) with 0≤y<b(t), V is smooth in y and continuously differentiable in t, Vy(t,0)=0, and

Below the bound, the value is smooth and solves the backward equation.

Work with the signed value U(t,x)=V(t,|x|)−∫0tc(u)du, so a rectangle can contain x=0: stopped at the exit from a closed rectangle inside the continuation set, it is a martingale, and the uniformly parabolic Dirichlet problem there has a smooth solution equal to it. So V is smooth in y, continuously differentiable in t, Vy(t,0)=0, and Vt+LV=c. (The paper extends the cost to t<0 by c(0), so t=0 is an interior time.)

Step 2 of 5

Freeze the optimal rule from one start, and use it from other start times.

Fix (t,y) below the bound and freeze its optimal stopping time τ=τt,y∗. For any start time t′, using that same τ earns J(t′)=Ey[g(Yτ)−∫0τc(t′+s)ds], so J(t′)≤V(t′,y), with equality at t′=t.

Step 3 of 5

Moving the start changes the cost paid over the whole decision, but its derivative involves only the costs at the two ends.

Differentiate: ddt′∫0τc(t′+s)ds=c(t′+τ)−c(t′), so J′(t)=c(t)−Eyc(t+τ). (The difference quotients are bounded by 2cmax, so the derivative passes inside the expectation.)

Step 4 of 5

A curve that stays below another and touches it has the same slope there.

V−J≥0 has a minimum at t, and both are differentiable there, so Vt(t,y)=J′(t)=c(t)−Ey[c(t+τ∗)].

Step 5 of 5

Subtract from the backward equation.

From Vt+LV=c: LV(t,y)=Ey[c(t+τt,y∗)]. The value's curvature term is the expected cost at the moment of decision.

The proof, in Appendix A.2

The continuation set C={(t,y):V>g}={y<b(t)} is open. Work with the signed value U(t,x)=V(t,|x|)−∫0tc(u)du on the open set {|x|<b(t)}, which contains x=0. Before the optimal stopping time, the value process is a martingale (the standing facts above), so for any closed rectangle R inside this set, U(t+s∧σ,Xs∧σ) is a martingale, where σ is the exit time of (t+s,Xs) from R. The operator ∂t+12∂x2+tanh⁡(x)∂x is uniformly parabolic with smooth coefficients, so the Dirichlet problem on R with the continuous data U on its parabolic boundary has a solution that is smooth inside R and continuous up to its boundary, and by the martingale property it equals U (as in Peskir and Shiryaev, 2006, Sec. 7.1). Hence U is smooth in the interior, even in x, and Ut+12Uxx+tanh⁡(x)Ux=0. Returning to V, it is smooth in y, continuously differentiable in t, Vy(t,0)=0, and Vt+LV=c.

Fix (t,y)∈C and τ=τt,y∗. For every t′,

(31)V(t′,y)≥J(t′):=Ey[g(Yτ)−∫0τc(t′+s)ds],

with equality at t′=t. The difference quotients of J are dominated by 2cmax, and ddt′∫0τc(t′+s)ds=c(t′+τ)−c(t′), so J′(t)=c(t)−Eyc(t+τ). Since V−J≥0 has a minimum at t and both are differentiable there, Vt(t,y)=J′(t). The second identity follows from Vt+LV=c.

Proposition 3: regularity

Three properties of the bound that the paper proves rather than assumes: (a) the value of waiting, W=V−g, grows at least quadratically below the bound, W(t,y)≥cmin(b(t)−y)2; (b) the bound is Hölder continuous in time with exponent 12; (c) smooth fit: the value's slope meets g′ at the bound. Parts (a) and (b) are the paper's own. For (c), the paper says its argument is that of De Angelis and Peskir (2020), specialized to a one-dimensional diffusion whose boundary points are regular by (b): a path started just below the bound crosses it almost at once, by the law of the iterated logarithm.

(a) By Lemma 2 and Lg=0, LW=LV≥cmin below the bound, so (cosh2⁡yWy)′≥2cmincosh2⁡y.

Step 3 of 5

At one time's bound, the other time's value of waiting is caught between a floor and a cap.

(b) Suppose b(t′)>b(t) and look at y=b(t). There W(t,y)=0, while (a) at time t′ gives W(t′,y)≥cmin(b(t′)−b(t))2. Lemma 1(d) caps the difference at (cmax−cmin)|t′−t|. So cmin(b(t′)−b(t))2≤(cmax−cmin)|t′−t|.

Step 4 of 5

A path that starts just below the bound crosses it almost at once.

(c) By (b), the bound can rise by at most Ks in time s, with K=1+(cmax−cmin)/cmin. Start a coupled path at b−ϵ: since its drift is nonnegative, it is at least b−ϵ+Bs, and by the law of the iterated logarithm Bs exceeds 2Ks at arbitrarily small s. So the path crosses the bound almost at once: τϵ→0.

Step 5 of 5

Compare the starts at the bound and just below it under one stopping time: the slopes match.

Since τϵ is a stopping time for both starts, V(t,b)−V(t,b−ϵ)≥E[g(Yτϵ0)−g(Yτϵϵ)], and the integrand is never negative, because Yϵ≤Y0 and g is increasing; so leaving out an event only lowers the right side. On the event that the lower path doesn't reach 0 first (no reflection), the two paths stay at least ϵ apart, and since g′ is decreasing, the integrand is at least ϵg′(Yτϵ0). As ϵ→0, that event has probability tending to 1 and Yτϵ0→b, so lim infϵ→0[V(t,b)−V(t,b−ϵ)]/ϵ≥g′(b), and W(t,b−ϵ)/ϵ→0. Because cosh2⁡yWy is nondecreasing and Wy≤0, Wy has a limit at the bound, and the mean value theorem makes it 0: Vy→g′(b). That is smooth fit.

The proof, in Appendix A.3

(a) Fix t and write b=b(t) and W=V−g on [0,b). By Lemma 2 and Lg=0, LW≥cmin, so (cosh2⁡yWy)′=2cosh2⁡yLW≥2cmincosh2⁡y. For y<z<b, integrating and using Wy(z)≤0 (Lemma 1(a)),

(32)−cosh2⁡yWy(y)≥2cmin∫yzcosh2⁡udu≥2cmincosh2⁡y(z−y).

Letting z→b gives −Wy(y)≥2cmin(b−y). Integrating from y to b, with W continuous and W(t,b)=0, gives W(t,y)≥cmin(b−y)2.

(b) Let t,t′≥0 with b(t′)>b(t), and put y=b(t). Then W(t,y)=0, and by (a) at time t′, W(t′,y)≥cmin(b(t′)−b(t))2. By Lemma 1(d), W(t′,y)−W(t,y)=V(t′,y)−V(t,y)≤(cmax−cmin)|t′−t|. Exchanging the roles of t and t′ covers the other case.

(c) Fix t, write b=b(t) and K=1+(cmax−cmin)/cmin, so b(t+s)≤b+Ks by (b). For 0≤ϵ<b, let Yϵ start from b−ϵ, driven by the same B, and τϵ=τt,b−ϵ∗. Since tanh≥0 on [0,∞) and ℓ≥0, Ysϵ≥b−ϵ+Bs. By the law of the iterated logarithm, almost surely there are arbitrarily small s>0 with Bs>2Ks, and at such s, Ysϵ−b(t+s)>Ks−ϵ, which is positive once ϵ<Ks. So τϵ→0 almost surely as ϵ→0.

Since τϵ is a stopping time for both Y0 and Yϵ,

(33)V(t,b)−V(t,b−ϵ)≥E[g(Yτϵ0)−g(Yτϵϵ)].

The integrand is nonnegative, because Yϵ≤Y0 and g is increasing. On the event Aϵ that Yϵ does not reach 0 before τϵ, there is no local time, so Y0−Yϵ=ϵ+∫(tanh⁡Y0−tanh⁡Yϵ)≥ϵ up to τϵ, and since g′ is decreasing on [0,∞) the integrand is at least ϵg′(Yτϵ0). As ϵ→0, P(Aϵ)→1 and Yτϵ0→b, so by dominated convergence lim infϵ→0[V(t,b)−V(t,b−ϵ)]/ϵ≥g′(b), that is, W(t,b−ϵ)/ϵ→0. Finally, cosh2⁡yWy is nondecreasing on [0,b) and Wy≤0, so Wy(t,y) has a limit L≤0 as y↑b. By the mean value theorem, W(t,b−ϵ)/ϵ=−Wy(t,ξϵ) for some ξϵ∈(b−ϵ,b), so L=0, which is smooth fit. This is the argument of De Angelis and Peskir (2020), specialized to a one-dimensional diffusion whose boundary points are regular by (b).

Lemma 6: two descriptions of the kernel

Fix a constant cost c0 and its flat bound b0=B(c0). The kernel w is the survival flux of the decision time at b0, normalized to total 1. The lemma gives (a) the flux as a series of positive exponentials, (b) a second description, as the law of the decision time when the start is drawn from π0(y)=4c0cosh2⁡y on [0,b0], and (c) the kernel's Laplace transform in closed form. The proof is the paper's own. It uses an h-transform to Brownian motion, an expansion in Dirichlet eigenfunctions, an ordinary differential equation for the transform, and the fact that two probability measures with the same Laplace transform are equal; of the paper's other results, it uses only the flat bound's equation (9). The explicit kernel and its transform are new, to the paper's knowledge.

Step 1 of 5

Undo the drift: the evidence is a Brownian motion, reweighted.

X is a Brownian motion h-transformed by h(s,x)=e−s/2cosh⁡x, so Px(τ0>s)=e−s/2cosh⁡xEx[cosh⁡Ws; τW>s] for a Brownian motion W that must stay in (−b,b).

Expand cosh⁡x in the even Dirichlet eigenfunctions cos⁡(κjx) on (−b,b), κj=(j+12)π/b, and differentiate at x=b: every term of the series (16) is positive.

Step 3 of 5

The transform of the decision time solves a second-order equation.

For the transform, u(x)=Exe−λτ0 solves 12u″+tanh⁡(x)u′=λu with u(±b)=1, so u=χ(x)/χ(b) with χ(x)=cosh⁡(rx)/cosh⁡x and r=2λ+1.

Step 4 of 5

Integrate over time to get the flux's transform, and normalize.

Since ∫0∞e−λsPx(τ0>s)ds=(1−u(x))/λ, the flux's transform is n~(λ)=χ′(b)/(λχ(b))=[rtanh⁡(rb)−tanh⁡b]/λ, and n~(0)=tanh⁡b+bsech2b=1/(2c0cosh2⁡b) by the constant-cost equation. Normalizing gives (a) and (c).

For (b), integrate Eye−λτ0 against π0(y)=4c0cosh2⁡y: the result is 4c0cosh2⁡b[rtanh⁡(rb)−tanh⁡b]/(r2−1), which is w~(λ) because r2−1=2λ. Two probability measures with the same Laplace transform are equal.

Theorem 7: the first-order theorem

For a cost c0+εγ(t), with c0>0 and γ continuous with |γ|≤M, the bound moves away from b0, to first order in ε, by εB′(c0)(w⋆γ)(t): the slope of the flat bound times the kernel's weighted average of the change still to come. The limit is uniform on bounded time intervals, and on all of [0,∞) if γ is uniformly continuous; for a Hölder continuous γ with exponent α, the remainder is O(|ε|1+α), uniformly on [0,∞). The theorem covers small, continuous changes around a constant cost on an infinite horizon; large changes, discontinuous steps, and deadlines lie outside it.

The proof is the paper's own: subtract the exact equations for the two costs, bracket the decision time between the hitting times of two fixed levels, and divide by ε. That the first-order change is a weighted average of the future change is not new: specializing Stojanovic's (1997) perturbation formula to this model at a constant cost formally gives that form. What the paper claims, to its knowledge, is the explicit kernel, its transform, and the proof for this model on an infinite horizon.

Theorem 7.

Let γ be continuous with |γ|≤M, let cε=c0+εγ, and let bε be the optimal bound for cε. Then, as ε→0,

(18)bε(t)−b0ε⟶β(t):=B′(c0)(w⋆γ)(t)

uniformly for t in compact sets, and uniformly on [0,∞) if γ is uniformly continuous. If γ is Hölder continuous with exponent α∈(0,1], then bε(t)=b0+εβ(t)+O(|ε|1+α) uniformly on [0,∞); in particular, the remainder is O(ε2) when γ is Lipschitz.

By Lemma 1(c) and the smoothness of B, |bε−b0|≤a|ε| for a constant a.

So two fixed levels bracket the decision time, and both close on τ0.

For starts below b0−a|ε|, the decision time τε lies between the hitting times of the fixed levels b0±a|ε|. Both converge almost surely to τ0, the hitting time of b0.

γ is uniformly continuous on compact sets and the bracketing times don't depend on t, so, on the common coupling, almost surely supt≤T|γ(t+τε)−γ(t+τ0)|→0; the thin strip near the bound adds O(|ε|). Dominated convergence gives Iε→I0=∫0b0cosh2⁡yEy[γ(t+τ0)]dy=(w⋆γ)(t)/(4c0), by Lemma 6(b).

The left side is c0cosh2⁡(ξ)(bε−b0) for some ξ between b0 and bε (mean value theorem). Divide by ε: (bε−b0)/ε→−(w⋆γ)/(4c02cosh2⁡b0)=B′(c0)(w⋆γ), uniformly on [0,T].

If the change is Hölder, the remainder has a rate.

If |γ(u)−γ(v)|≤L|u−v|α, Jensen's inequality bounds |Eγ(t+τε)−Eγ(t+τ0)| by L[E(σ+−σ−)]α, and E(σ+−σ−)=O(|ε|) from Eyσz=ztanh⁡z−ytanh⁡y. With the strip, which contributes O(|ε|), this gives |Iε(t)−I0(t)|=O(|ε|α) uniformly in t≥0, and with 1/cosh2⁡ξ−1/cosh2⁡b0=O(|ε|), δ(t)/ε−β(t)=O(|ε|α) uniformly in t≥0.

Corollary 8 and Corollary 9: the transfer function and the limits

Both read the kernel's transform. Corollary 8: a sinusoidal change in the cost moves the bound, to first order, by a sinusoid of the same frequency, whose swing is |w~(−iω)|<1 times the per-moment response's, with a phase lead between 0∘ and 90∘. Corollary 9: (a) very slow changes recover the per-moment rule; (b) the mean look-ahead has a closed form, tends to 12 as time becomes free and to 0 as it becomes expensive, and peaks at about 0.619, near c0≈ 0.035, a maximum the paper finds numerically; (c) at high frequency, the swing falls like ω−1/2, and the lead tends to 45∘. Corollary 8 (Transfer function).

For a sinusoidal cost γ(t)=Re(Γeiωt) with ω>0,

(21)β(t)=Re(B′(c0)w~(−iω)Γeiωt).

So the bound's swing is |w~(−iω)|<1 times the swing of the per-moment response B′(c0)γ, and the bound leads that response by the phase arg⁡w~(−iω)∈(0∘,90∘).

The signs come from the series (16): w~(−iω) is a positive combination of terms 1/(αj−iω) with αj>0, each with positive real and imaginary parts.

  • (a)

    Slow changes. w~(0)=1, so very slow changes recover the per-moment rule.

    Fast changes. As ω→∞, |w~(−iω)|∼2c0cosh2⁡(b0)2/ω and arg⁡w~(−iω)→45∘.

Corollary 8.

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 4

A wave through the kernel comes out as the same wave, scaled and turned.

For γ(t)=eiωt, (w⋆γ)(t)=∫0∞w(s)eiω(t+s)ds, which is eiωtw~(−iω). Taking real parts with B′(c0) and Γ gives β(t)=Re(B′(c0)w~(−iω)Γeiωt).

Step 2 of 4

Write the transform as a sum of simple terms, one per exponential in the series.

From the series (16), w~(−iω)=∑jaj/(αj−iω) with aj>0, αj=(1+κj2)/2, and ∑jaj/αj=1 (the value at ω=0).

Step 3 of 4

At any frequency above 0, every term points up and to the right.

Each term 1/(αj−iω)=(αj+iω)/(αj2+ω2) has positive real and imaginary parts, so the sum's phase lies strictly between 0∘ and 90∘.

Step 4 of 4

Every term is shorter than it was at zero frequency, so the sum's modulus is less than 1.

Each term has modulus aj/|αj−iω|<aj/αj for ω>0, so |w~(−iω)|<∑jaj/αj=1. (The paper also notes the terms have different phases, which makes the triangle inequality strict.)

Chapter 7 draws each step beside its live plate “The terms of the transform”, in A sinusoid in, a sinusoid out.

Corollary 9, parts (a) and (b).

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 4

Slow changes: the transform at zero is 1.

(a) w~(0)=∫0∞w(s)ds=1 because w is normalized: at zero frequency the weighted average is the value itself, which is the per-moment rule.

Step 2 of 4

The mean is minus the transform's slope at zero, and an average over starts.

(b) m(c0)=∫0∞sw(s)ds=−w~′(0). By Lemma 6(b), it is also ∫0b0π0(y)Eyτ0dy, the mean decision time from the start law π0.

Step 3 of 4

The mean time from each start has a closed form; integrate it.

Eyτ0=b0tanh⁡b0−ytanh⁡y solves Lm=−1 with m′(0)=0 and m(b0)=0. Integrating against 4c0cosh2⁡y, with the constant-cost equation, gives (22): m(c0)=c0[12sinh⁡2b0−b0+2b02tanh⁡b0].

Step 4 of 4

Half a unit when time is free, nothing when it is expensive; the peak in between is numerical.

The second form of (22), m=12+2b0(b0tanh⁡b0−1)sinh⁡2b0+2b0, shows m→12 as b0→∞ (c0→0). As c0→∞, b0∼1/(4c0) and m∼23b02→0. The maximum is found numerically.

Chapter 7 draws each step beside its live plate “The look-ahead, step by step”, in How far ahead the bound looks.

Corollary 9, part (c).

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 5

At a high frequency, r is close to (1−i)ω.

(c) At λ=−iω, r=1−2iω, and −2iω=(1−i)ω, so r∼(1−i)ω as ω→∞.

Step 2 of 5

The hyperbolic tangent approaches 1.

The real part of rb0 is about b0ω, which grows without bound, so tanh⁡(rb0)→1, exponentially fast.

Step 3 of 5

What is left has a gain like ω−1/2 and a phase of 45∘.

So w~(−iω)∼2c0cosh2⁡b0(1−i)ω/(−iω), which is 2c0cosh2⁡b0(1+i)/ω: modulus 2c0cosh2⁡b02/ω, phase 45∘. The −tanh⁡b0 in the closed form is smaller by a factor of ω.

Step 4 of 5

A transform like λ−1/2 comes from a kernel like s−1/2.

Near s=0, the terms of the series (16) add up to n(s)≈2/(πs), so w(s)≈2c0cosh2⁡b02/(πs), whose transform is 2c0cosh2⁡b02/λ: the same behavior at high frequency.

Step 5 of 5

Half of an integration: fast changes are smoothed, not ignored.

Integrating over time divides a wave's swing by ω and delays it by 90∘. A kernel like s−1/2 does half of each: its gain falls like ω−1/2 and its phase tends to 45∘ (a lead, since the kernel averages the future). An exponential kernel with the same mean falls like ω−1.

Proposition 13: the weighted rule near a constant cost

The weighted look-ahead rule (Definition 12 · The weighted look-ahead rule) sets its bound by an equation in which the bound appears on both sides. For a cost c0+εγ, with γ continuous, |γ|≤M, and |ε| small, the proposition shows that the equation has exactly one solution in [B(c0+|ε|M),B(c0−|ε|M)] at each time, and that the solution matches the optimal bound to first order. The per-moment rule's error, divided by ε, instead tends to B′(c0)(γ−w⋆γ), which is identically zero only for a constant γ. The same proof shows that the averaged-cost rule, bavg(t)=B((wc(t)⋆c)(t)), is exact to first order. The proof is the paper's own. For large changes, the paper notes, the equation can have more than one solution.

In the claim map, for Proposition 13 · Near a constant cost, the rule is well defined and first-order exact:

  • It uses Definition 12 · The weighted look-ahead rule; Theorem 7 · The first-order theorem; Lemma 6 · Two descriptions of the kernel; Corollary 8 · Transfer function.
  • What uses it: The per-moment rule's bound error is first order; the corrected rule's is smaller; Conjecture 11 · Leading-order loss; What is new, to the paper's knowledge.

In the claim map, for The averaged-cost rule:

  • It uses Theorem 7 · The first-order theorem; The kernel w (survival flux at the bound).
  • What uses it: Held-out schedules (210, seed 20261111) and five more rules.
The definition and the statement, in Section 5
Definition 12 (Weighted look-ahead).

For a level b>0, let wb be the kernel (14) computed for the interval (−b,b), and let w0 be a unit mass at s=0. The weighted look-ahead bound bw(t) solves

(25)bw(t)=∫0∞wbw(t)(s)B(c(t+s))ds,

with B(∞)=0, so that bw=0 at and after a deadline.

Proposition 13 (Near a constant cost, the rule is well defined and first-order exact).

For c=c0+εγ with γ continuous, |γ|≤M, and |ε| small, (25) has a unique solution in [B(c0+|ε|M),B(c0−|ε|M)] at each t, and

(26)bw(t)=b0+εβ(t)+O(ε2)

uniformly in t. Hence (bw−bε)/ε→0 locally uniformly, while (bpm−bε)/ε→B′(c0)(γ−w⋆γ), which is not identically zero unless γ is constant. If γ is Lipschitz, bw−bε=O(ε2) uniformly.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 599–622

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 6

The map sends the interval into itself.

Let I=[B(c0+|ε|M),B(c0−|ε|M)] and Tε(b;t)=∫0∞wb(s)B(c(t+s))ds. Since B is decreasing and each wb is a probability density, Tε(⋅;t) maps I into I.

Step 2 of 6

Every kernel integrates to one, so its change in the level integrates to zero.

From the series (16) with b in place of b0, b↦wb is continuously differentiable into L1 on compact sets of levels, with ∥∂bwb∥L1 bounded on I, and ∫∂bwb=0 because every wb integrates to one.

Step 3 of 6

So the map is nearly flat: a contraction, with one fixed point.

|∂bTε(b;t)|=|∫∂bwb(s)[B(c(t+s))−b0]ds|≤∥∂bwb∥L1supu|B(c(u))−b0|=O(|ε|), so for small |ε| the map is a contraction on I with a unique fixed point.

Step 4 of 6

Expand to first order: the fixed point has the theorem's first-order term.

Expand B(c(t+s))=b0+εB′(c0)γ(t+s)+O(ε2), and use |bw(t)−b0|=O(ε) and the Lipschitz dependence of wb on b: bw(t)=b0+εB′(c0)(wb0⋆γ)(t)+O(ε2), uniformly in t.

Step 5 of 6

Compare with the theorem: divided by ε, the weighted rule's error goes to 0 (and is O(ε²) for a Lipschitz γ); the per-moment rule's doesn't.

By Theorem 7, (bw−bε)/ε→0 locally uniformly, while (bpm−bε)/ε→B′(c0)(γ−w⋆γ); for a Lipschitz γ, bw−bε=O(ε2). The same L1 bound shows that bavg is exact to first order.

Step 6 of 6

Only a constant change averages to itself.

If γ=w⋆γ for a bounded continuous γ, extend γ to the whole line by renewal so that Γ=w⋆Γ everywhere. Its distributional Fourier transform is supported where w~(−iξ)=1, which by Corollary 8 is only ξ=0; so Γ is a polynomial and, being bounded, a constant.

Chapter 8 draws each step beside its live plate “A map that is nearly flat”, in Why it is first-order exact.

The proof, in Appendix A.8

Let I=[B(c0+|ε|M),B(c0−|ε|M)] and Tε(b;t)=∫0∞wb(s)B(c(t+s))ds for b∈I. Since B is decreasing and each wb is a probability density, Tε(⋅;t) maps I into I. The kernel for level b is the series (16) with b in place of b0, divided by its total mass tanh⁡b+bsech2b, which is positive and smooth in b. Its terms qj(b,s)=(2/b)[κj2/(1+κj2)]e−(1+κj2)s/2, with κj=(j+12)π/b, have ∂bqj=(qj/b)[sκj2−1−2/(1+κj2)], and on a compact set of levels both ∥qj∥L1 and ∥∂bqj∥L1 are at most a constant times (j+12)−2. So b↦wb is continuously differentiable into L1 on compact subsets of (0,∞), with ∥∂bwb∥L1 bounded on I, and ∫∂bwb=0 because each wb integrates to one. Hence

(39)|∂bTε(b;t)|=|∫∂bwb(s)[B(c(t+s))−b0]ds|≤∥∂bwb∥L1supu|B(c(u))−b0|=O(|ε|),

so Tε(⋅;t) is a contraction on I for small |ε|, with a unique fixed point. Expanding B(c(t+s))=b0+εB′(c0)γ(t+s)+O(ε2) and using |bw(t)−b0|=O(ε) and the Lipschitz dependence of wb on b gives bw(t)=b0+εB′(c0)(wb0⋆γ)(t)+O(ε2) uniformly. The statements about (bw−bε)/ε and (bpm−bε)/ε follow from Theorem 7, and so does bw−bε=O(ε2) for a Lipschitz γ. The same L1 bound shows that bavg is exact to first order: wc(t) is the kernel for the level B(c(t))=b0+O(ε), so ∥wc(t)−wc0∥L1=O(ε), and since both kernels integrate to one, (wc(t)⋆c)(t)−(wc0⋆c)(t)=∫(wc(t)−wc0)(s)[c(t+s)−c0]ds=O(ε2), so bavg=b0+εβ+O(ε2).

Finally, if γ=w⋆γ for a bounded continuous γ, then γ is constant. Extend γ to the whole line: for x<0, let Γ(x)=E[γ(x+SN)], where Sn is a sum of n independent steps with density w and N is the first n with x+Sn≥0, and let Γ=γ on [0,∞). Since the steps are positive, N is finite, and conditioning on the first step gives Γ=w⋆Γ on the whole line, with Γ bounded. The kernel has exponential tails, so its Fourier transform is smooth, and the distributional Fourier transform of Γ is supported where w~(−iξ)=1, which by Corollary 8 is only ξ=0. So Γ is a polynomial and, being bounded, a constant.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 1476–1513

Proposition 10: second-order loss

A bound that misses the optimum loses reward only at second order. Fix a start y0∈[0,b0) and a>0: for all small ε, every policy that stops at a continuous bound within a|ε| of b0 earns at most Cε2 less than the optimal policy for the cost c0+εγ. The per-moment rule and the weighted look-ahead both qualify, so both lose O(ε2). The proof is the paper's own: the value of waiting is at most quadratic near the bound, by smooth fit, and a path spends little time in a thin band next to an absorbing level. How much each rule loses at leading order is Conjecture 11, which the paper checks numerically but does not prove. The paper places this proof last in Appendix A, after that of Proposition 13.

In the claim map:

  • It uses Lemma 1 · Structure; Proposition 3 · Regularity (nondegeneracy, Hölder continuity, smooth fit); The constant-cost bound B(c).
  • What uses it: Conjecture 11 · Leading-order loss; In reward, the per-moment rule is already close to optimal; How the loss scales with the size of the change.
The statement, in Section 4.4
Proposition 10 (Second-order loss).

Fix a starting point y0∈[0,b0) and a>0. There is a constant C such that, for all small ε, every policy that stops when Y first reaches a continuous bound b^ with ∥b^−b0∥∞≤a|ε| earns at most Cε2 less than the optimal policy for the cost c0+εγ.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 546–552

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 4

Both decision times are caught between two fixed levels.

Let A=max(a,a0), where a0|ε| bounds the optimal bound's own distance from b0 (Lemma 1(c)). Both the policy's decision time τ^ and the optimal one lie between the hitting times τ± of b0±A|ε|: τ−≤τ^≤τ+.

Step 2 of 4

At the constant cost, the shortfall has two parts.

Itô's formula for V0 gives the policy's shortfall V0(y0)−J0(b^) as E[W0(Yτ^)]+c0E∫0τ^1{Ys≥b0}ds, the waiting value left where it stops and the cost of time spent above b0.

Step 3 of 4

Both parts are of order ε².

Yτ^ is within A|ε| of b0, where W0≤C(b0−y)2 by smooth fit and a bounded second derivative. The expected time spent in a band of width A|ε| next to an absorbing level is O(ε2). The same holds for the optimal policy of cε.

Step 4 of 4

Changing the cost changes both rewards by nearly the same amount.

The perturbation changes each policy's reward by −εE∫0τγ. Between the two policies, these changes differ by at most |ε|M(Eτ+−Eτ−)=O(ε2), since Ey0σz=ztanh⁡z−y0tanh⁡y0 is smooth in the level z.

Chapter 7 draws each step beside its live plate “A thin band at the bound”, in Why the reward barely moves.

The proof, in Appendix A.9

By Lemma 1(c), ∥bε−b0∥∞≤a0|ε| for a constant a0; let A=max(a,a0). Let τ^ be the decision time of the policy with bound b^, and τ± the hitting times of b0±A|ε|; then τ−≤τ^≤τ+, and the same holds for the optimal time τε. Write J0 for rewards under the constant cost c0 and V0,W0 for its value and waiting value. First, at constant cost, Itô's formula for the C1, piecewise C2 function V0 gives

(40)V0(y0)−J0(b^)=E[W0(Yτ^)]+c0E∫0τ^1{Ys≥b0}ds.

The first term is at most Cε2, because Yτ^ lies within A|ε| of b0, where W0≤C(b0−y)2 by smooth fit and the bounded second derivative. The second is at most c0∫b0b0+A|ε|G(y0,z)dz, with the Green's function of Y killed at b0+A|ε|, which vanishes linearly at that level; so it is also O(ε2). The same holds for the optimal policy of cε. Second, the perturbation εγ changes the reward of each policy by −εE∫0τγ(s)ds, and these changes differ between the two policies by at most |ε|ME|τ^−τε|≤|ε|M(Eτ+−Eτ−)=O(ε2), since Ey0σz=ztanh⁡z−y0tanh⁡y0 is smooth in z.

Appendix B: unequal rewards at a constant cost

When a correct + earns r+ and a correct − earns r−, the problem can't be folded at 0, and the decision maker waits while the evidence lies between two bounds ℓ<h, around the point x∗ where the two choices earn the same. Appendix B derives the two bounds for a constant cost: the value's equation integrates once, as for the flat bound, smooth fit at each bound gives one equation, and value matching across the interval gives a third. It takes the waiting region to be an interval around x∗ and uses smooth fit at both ends; the paper doesn't prove these separately for unequal rewards (Proposition 3 is for equal rewards). What Section 7.2 builds on these bounds, one first-order kernel for each bound, is formal: “We have not made it rigorous for unequal rewards.” The claim map's entry covers both parts, and its uses, below, are those of the first-order argument.

In the claim map:

  • It uses Lemma 2 · Envelope identity; Proposition 3 · Regularity (nondegeneracy, Hölder continuity, smooth fit); Theorem 7 · The first-order theorem.
  • What uses it: Limitations, as the paper states them.
The setting, in Section 7.2

Suppose a correct “+” choice earns r+>0 and a correct “−” choice earns r−>0, with errors earning nothing. The reduction to |X| fails, and the continuation region is an interval (ℓ(t),h(t)) that contains the indifference point x∗=12log⁡(r−/r+). For a constant cost, the two bounds solve a pair of explicit equations (Appendix B).

…

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 1064–1067

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 5

With unequal rewards, the problem can't be folded at 0: the evidence is followed on both sides, and stopping earns the better of the two choices.

A correct + earns r+ and a correct − earns r−, so stopping at x earns G(x)=max(r+g(x), r−(1−g(x))). For a constant cost c, the decision maker waits while ℓ<x<h, an interval around x∗=12log⁡(r−/r+), where the two choices earn the same.

Step 2 of 5

Between the bounds, the value solves the same equation as for equal rewards, and it integrates once, with a constant left free.

X has the generator L=12∂x2+tanh⁡(x)∂x, so on (ℓ,h), LV=c becomes (cosh2⁡xV′)′=2ccosh2⁡x, and cosh2⁡xV′(x)=cS(x)+K with S(x)=x+12sinh⁡2x. For equal rewards, the reflecting center gave V′(0)=0 and so K=0; here nothing fixes K yet.

Step 3 of 5

Smooth fit at each bound gives one equation each.

At h the value meets r+g, whose slope is r+g′(h)=r+/(2cosh2⁡h); at ℓ it meets r−(1−g), whose slope is −r−/(2cosh2⁡ℓ). Multiplied by cosh2, the two slopes give cS(h)+K=12r+ and cS(ℓ)+K=−12r−.

Step 4 of 5

Value matching gives the third: across the interval, the value changes by exactly as much as the reward for stopping does.

Since S′=2cosh2⁡x, integrating by parts gives ∫Ssech2xdx=Stanh⁡x−12cosh⁡2x, so A, which is c(Stanh⁡x−12cosh⁡2x) plus Ktanh⁡x, has A′=V′. Then V(h)−V(ℓ)=G(h)−G(ℓ) reads A(h)−A(ℓ)=r+g(h)−r−(1−g(ℓ)). With step 3, that is three equations for ℓ, h, and K.

Step 5 of 5

Equal rewards give back the flat bound.

For r+=r−=1, h=−ℓ and K=0 satisfy both equations of step 3 when cS(h)=12, which is sinh⁡(2h)+2h=1/c, so h=−ℓ=B(c). Value matching holds too: A is then even, and 1−g(−h)=g(h), so both sides of step 4 are 0. For a common reward r, dividing the equations by r gives h=−ℓ=B(c/r).

These steps are this appendix's own. Chapter 11 draws the same derivation, in steps of its own, beside its live plate “Appendix B, a step at a time”, in Unequal rewards: two bounds.

The derivation, in Appendix B

With rewards r±>0 and a constant cost c, the stopping reward is G(x)=max(r+g(x),r−(1−g(x))) and the continuation region is (ℓ,h) with ℓ<x∗<h. On it, (cosh2⁡xV′)′=2ccosh2⁡x, so cosh2⁡xV′(x)=cS(x)+K with S(x)=x+12sinh⁡2x and a constant K. Smooth fit at both ends gives

(41)cS(h)+K=12r+,cS(ℓ)+K=−12r−,

and value matching, V(h)−V(ℓ)=r+g(h)−r−(1−g(ℓ)), gives

(42)A(h)−A(ℓ)=r+g(h)−r−(1−g(ℓ)),A(x)=c(S(x)tanh⁡x−12cosh⁡2x)+Ktanh⁡x.

For r+=r−=1, these reduce to h=−ℓ=B(c) and K=0; for a common reward r, h=−ℓ=B(c/r).

Exercises

Worked answers are folded under each question. Nothing is gated.

  1. Where do the proofs use cmin>0?

    Worked answer

    The standing assumptions drop stopping times with an infinite mean because their cost is infinite, which needs a cost of at least cmin>0. The optimal-stopping fact caps decisions at b¯=B(cmin), which is finite only for cmin>0 (by (9), B(c)→∞ as c→0), with Eyσ=b¯tanh⁡b¯−ytanh⁡y<∞. Lemma 1(c) bounds b(t) above by the same B(cmin). In Proposition 3, (a) gives W≥cmin(b−y)2, which says nothing when cmin=0; the Hölder constant of (b), (cmax−cmin)/cmin, is infinite there; and (c) uses that constant. The exact equation and Theorem 7 rest on smooth fit; Theorem 7 also needs c0>0, so that c0+εγ stays between two positive constants for small ε.

  2. Which of the results above does Theorem 7 use directly, and which only through them?

    Worked answer

    By the claim map, directly: The slope of the constant-cost bound; Lemma 1 · Structure; Proposition 4 · Exact equation for the bound; Lemma 6 · Two descriptions of the kernel. Only through those: The reflected process Y = |X|, its generator, and three facts about g; The constant-cost bound B(c); Strong solutions of the reflected equation; Optimal stopping applies after capping the bound; Lemma 2 · Envelope identity; Proposition 3 · Regularity (nondegeneracy, Hölder continuity, smooth fit). So the theorem rests on every result before it on this page. Of the results it uses directly, only Lemma 6 and the slope (10) are not already behind the exact equation, which is the finding at the top of the page.

  3. Which steps of Appendix A does the paper attribute to other work?

    Worked answer

    Four citations, in the opening facts and in the proofs of Lemma 2 and Proposition 3: Skorokhod's lemma, for strong solutions (Revuz and Yor, 1999); the optimal-stopping theorem for continuous gains (Peskir and Shiryaev, 2006, Ch. I, Thm. 2.2), applied after the paper's own capping argument; the Dirichlet-problem method behind the smoothness in Lemma 2 (as in Peskir and Shiryaev, 2006, Sec. 7.1); and the smooth-fit argument of Proposition 3(c), which the paper calls that of De Angelis and Peskir (2020), specialized to this diffusion. The rest of Appendix A and all of Appendix B cite no other work, though they use textbook facts by name (Itô's formula, the law of the iterated logarithm, dominated convergence, and Jensen's inequality, among others).

Common misreadings.

  • “The appendix proves every step from scratch.”The paper calls two facts standard and cites them, and it follows De Angelis and Peskir (2020) for smooth fit and Peskir and Shiryaev (2006) for the smoothness in Lemma 2. Each section above says what is the paper's own.
  • “The proofs cover deadlines and large steps.”The standing assumptions make the cost continuous and keep it between two positive constants, on an infinite horizon; the paper notes that Lemma 1(d) holds for any bounded measurable cost. Theorem 7, Proposition 13, and Proposition 10 are about small changes around a constant cost. A deadline makes the cost infinite. There, the paper's rules are heuristics, judged by measurement (Section 6).
  • “Appendix B proves the rule for unequal rewards.”It derives the two bounds for a constant cost. The first-order argument for unequal rewards in Section 7.2, one kernel for each bound, is formal; the paper checks it numerically.
